title: A plan no weighting can reach, with its proof

blocks.text: A city parks department has a small budget and a short list of projects: new trees, a pond, play courts and so on. Each costs money and adds two things the department reports on, square metres of tree canopy (shade) and extra visits a week, both to maximize. The council has asked for "the best plan at our weights", and the department suspects that the plan it would actually recommend is one no weights would ever pick. It wants to find such a plan and show the council a proof it can check by hand.
Write `unreachable(projects, budget)` in `parks.py`. A plan is any set of projects whose total cost is within `budget`. Return a triple `(plan, a, b)` of sets of project names, or `None`:

items: `plan` must be dominated by no allowed plan;
`a` and `b` must be allowed plans with less and more shade than `plan`, and the straight line from `a` to `b` must pass strictly above `plan` (more visits at `plan`'s shade);
return `None` only when every unbeaten plan is picked by some weighting.

blocks.text: An unbeaten plan that lies exactly on the straight line between two others counts as picked: at the share where those two tie, it ties with them, so that weighting makes it optimal (it is supported, lesson 8.1.2). Such a plan is never the answer, and when every unbeaten plan is a hull corner or on a straight stretch between corners, the answer is `None`. The proof's line must pass *strictly* above `plan`, as the second rule says.

The lists are short enough to try every set. Work it out on paper first: which points of the shade-visits picture can a weighted sum return, and why does a line from `a` to `b` above `plan` prove that no share picks `plan`? Then decide which two plans make a proof that always works.

cases.says: an unbeaten compromise plan is returned with two plans whose line passes above it
when every unbeaten plan is picked by some weighting, the answer is None
an unbeaten plan exactly on the line between two others is picked by a weighting, so the answer is None
a plan that costs exactly the budget is allowed
the proof's two plans are ones a weighting picks, not merely the nearest unbeaten plans

origin.section: No Weight Reaches a Point Below the Segment Between Its Supported Neighbours

concepts: a point below the segment between two feasible plans loses to one of them at every share
a supported point is returned by some weighted sum, an unsupported one by none
